title: YOUR HUSBAND HAS BEEN GONE FOR MONTHS. YOU STILL HAVE DESIRES. BUT DOES SATISFYING YOURSELF MEAN YOU’VE BETRAYED YOUR MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: YOUR HUSBAND HAS BEEN GONE FOR MONTHS. YOU STILL HAVE DESIRES. BUT DOES SATISFYING YOURSELF MEAN YOU’VE BETRAYED YOUR MARRIAGE?

The question many Christian wives are too ashamed to ask—and the biblical truth about sexual longing, loneliness, marital faithfulness, and the grace of Jesus Christ that could change how you see your body, your marriage, and your relationship with God.
The house is finally quiet.
The children are asleep. The dishes are done. The lights are off.
And there you are.
Alone in a bed that was never meant to feel this empty.

Your husband is hundreds, perhaps thousands, of miles away. Maybe he works overseas. Maybe he serves in the military. Maybe financial necessity has forced you into a marriage where love is measured through video calls, delayed messages, and the painful countdown to the next reunion.
You miss his voice.
You miss his arms around you.
You miss the ordinary things nobody warned you would become precious.
The warmth of another person beside you. The familiar sound of his breathing. The comfort of knowing that when the world becomes unbearable, you can reach across the bed and find him there.
But tonight, you reach across the bed.
And there is nobody.
Then something happens that makes you uncomfortable even admitting it.
Your body begins to long for intimacy.
Not necessarily for another man.
Not because you have stopped loving your husband.
Not because you want to destroy your marriage.
You simply miss the physical closeness that marriage once allowed you to enjoy without fear or shame.
And somewhere between loneliness, longing, and the silence of another sleepless night, a question enters your mind.
If I masturbate while my husband is away, am I betraying him?
Then comes another question.
Would God be disappointed in me?
And perhaps the most painful one of all:
Does having these desires mean something is wrong with my faith?
Before you bury that question beneath another layer of religious guilt, there is something you need to understand.
The Bible has much to say about sexual holiness, marital faithfulness, lust, self-control, and the goodness of marriage. But it does not explicitly say that every act of masturbation is adultery.
That distinction matters.
Because when we speak in God's name, we must be careful not to condemn what Scripture has not clearly condemned—or excuse what Scripture clearly identifies as sin.
And if you are going to wrestle with something this personal, you deserve more than frightening religious slogans.
You deserve the truth.
The kind of truth that does not flatter your flesh.
The kind that does not crush your soul.
The kind that leads you back to Jesus.
Because sometimes the deepest spiritual struggle is not between a woman and her desires.
Sometimes it is between what God actually said and what she has spent her entire life being afraid He said.
When God created humanity, He did not create the human body as something shameful.
Genesis 1:31 tells us that God saw everything He had made, and it was very good.
The Hebrew expression is טוֹב מְאֹד (tov me'od)—meaning "very good."
That declaration includes embodied human existence.
Your body is not an embarrassing accident that God reluctantly tolerates.
Your capacity for sexual desire is not, by itself, proof of spiritual corruption.
Sexual desire is part of human nature, though like every human appetite, it must be understood and governed within God's moral purposes.
And Scripture does not pretend that married people stop having sexual desires simply because their spouses are temporarily absent.
In fact, the apostle Paul spoke remarkably openly about the physical dimensions of marriage.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3, he writes:
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not describe marital intimacy as something only husbands need.
He does not portray a wife's sexual longing as shameful.
He recognizes that marriage includes mutual physical obligations, affection, and care.
The Greek word translated "conjugal rights" is ὀφειλή (opheilē), meaning something owed or due.
Within this context, Paul is describing the mutual responsibilities of spouses—not granting either person permission to demand sexual activity without consent.
The following verse makes the mutuality unmistakable.
"For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does." (1 Corinthians 7:4, ESV)
Read that second sentence again.
The husband's body is not presented as exclusively his own to use without consideration for his wife.
Paul speaks of reciprocal responsibility.
This was a strikingly mutual way to address marital intimacy.
And it challenges two harmful ideas.
The first is that a wife's sexual needs are somehow less legitimate than her husband's.
The second is that marriage gives either spouse unrestricted control over the other's body.
Neither idea faithfully captures Paul's teaching.
Biblical marital intimacy is meant to be shaped by love, mutual care, faithfulness, and willing participation—not coercion.
Then Paul continues:

"Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control." (1 Corinthians 7:5, ESV)
The Greek expression μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους (mē apostereite allēlous) means "do not deprive one another."
Paul is addressing the deliberate withholding of marital intimacy, especially in the context of abstinence for spiritual purposes.
He is not writing a detailed instruction manual for couples separated by military service, overseas employment, hospitalization, or other unavoidable circumstances.
That distinction is important.
A husband working abroad to provide for his family is not automatically guilty of depriving his wife in the sense Paul is addressing.
A wife who struggles with sexual longing during that separation is not automatically guilty of moral failure.
But Paul's words remind us that sexual needs within marriage should not simply be ignored.
Distance may be necessary.
Emotional abandonment is not.
A couple can be physically separated without ceasing to care for one another's emotional and relational needs.
And sometimes that care begins with a conversation both spouses are embarrassed to have.
"Love, I miss you. Not just talking to you. I miss being close to you. This separation is harder than I expected."
There is nothing ungodly about that confession.
It may be one of the most honest things you can say to the person you married.
But now we must face the question you came here to ask.
Is masturbation itself a betrayal of marriage?
Here is where biblical honesty becomes essential.
The Bible does not contain an explicit command that names masturbation and declares every instance of it sinful.
Some Christians argue that masturbation is inherently incompatible with God's design for sexuality because sexual expression belongs within the mutual union of husband and wife.
Others believe Scripture does not justify a universal prohibition, and that moral evaluation must consider the thoughts, intentions, habits, relationships, and circumstances involved.
These are genuine differences among Christians seeking to interpret Scripture faithfully.
We should not pretend the disagreement does not exist.
Nor should we claim that the Bible explicitly settles a question it does not directly address.
Consider a passage frequently brought into this discussion.
Genesis 38 tells the story of Onan.
When Onan was expected to fulfill his duty to provide offspring for his deceased brother, he deliberately prevented conception.
Genesis 38:9 describes his action.
For generations, some people have used this account to argue that masturbation is directly condemned in Scripture.
But the passage is not describing solitary masturbation.
It concerns Onan's refusal to fulfill a family obligation while engaging in sexual relations with Tamar.
The narrative identifies his conduct as wicked, and its context includes his deliberate refusal to provide offspring for his brother.
Using this passage as though it directly states that all masturbation is sinful goes beyond what the text actually says.
That does not automatically make masturbation morally permissible.
It simply means we must not force a biblical passage to answer a question it was not written to address.
And Christians should be especially careful about doing that.
Because spiritual authority becomes dangerous when human conclusions are presented as direct quotations from God.
Jesus Himself confronted religious leaders who elevated human traditions in ways that obscured God's commands.
In Mark 7:8, He says:
"You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men." (ESV)
That warning should make every Christian teacher humble.
We must never weaken God's holiness.
But we must also never invent commandments and then use them to terrify people into obedience.
Now consider another passage.
Matthew 5:28.
Jesus says:
"But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart." (ESV)
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) refers, in this context, to looking at a woman with the purpose of desiring her lustfully.
The surrounding teaching concerns adultery and the moral condition of the heart.
Jesus is exposing the false idea that a person can remain righteous simply because an outward act of adultery has not occurred.
He directs attention to deliberate, wrongful desire.
But we must distinguish between sexual desire itself and lustful intent.
A wife longing for her husband is not committing adultery simply because she desires sexual closeness.
A passing sexual thought is not automatically equivalent to deliberately cultivating fantasies about someone outside the marriage.
And an involuntary physical response is not necessarily a chosen act of sin.
These distinctions matter because Jesus is not teaching that the existence of sexual desire makes a person spiritually filthy.
He is teaching that the heart matters.
So the question becomes deeper than whether a particular physical action has occurred.
What is happening in your heart?
Are you deliberately fantasizing about someone other than your spouse?
Are you consuming pornography that trains you to view other people as objects for gratification?
Are you cultivating secret sexual attachments that undermine your marriage?
Are you using sexual stimulation compulsively to escape emotional pain that needs attention?
Are you violating an agreement you and your husband have made?
Or are you a lonely married woman trying to understand how to respond to a natural desire during a prolonged separation?
These situations are not morally identical.
And treating them as identical may prevent the kind of honest discernment that Christian maturity requires.
Pornography, for example, raises concerns that extend beyond the question of masturbation.
It can encourage lust directed toward people outside one's marriage, objectification, secrecy, exploitation, and patterns of behavior that damage trust.
Jesus' teaching about lust is directly relevant to deliberately cultivating adulterous desire.
But it does not follow that every bodily sensation, every sexual thought, or every instance of solitary sexual activity must be described as adultery.
The moral question requires more care than that.
And here is something else worth considering.
Marriage is not merely an arrangement in which two people promise never to touch anyone else.
Marriage is a covenant of faithfulness.
It includes trust, honesty, mutual responsibility, sacrifice, and love.
A person can avoid physical adultery and still wound a marriage through deception, cruelty, neglect, or emotional betrayal.
And a person can experience sexual frustration without being unfaithful.
This is why the conversation between husband and wife matters.
Some couples regard masturbation during prolonged separation as inconsistent with their understanding of marital sexual exclusivity.
Others, after prayerful consideration and honest discussion, do not regard every instance as a violation of their vows.
Neither spouse should simply assume the other shares the same convictions.
And neither should use Scripture as a weapon to control or humiliate the other.
A healthy conversation might begin with an uncomfortable but necessary question.
"How do we honor God and protect our marriage while we're apart?"
Not, "How much can I get away with?"
Not, "How can I hide this so you never find out?"
But, "How do we remain faithful to Christ and to each other when our circumstances are difficult?"
That is a much better question.
Because faithfulness is not merely the absence of scandal.
It is the presence of covenant love.
And sometimes covenant love requires a husband to understand that the wife he left at home is carrying burdens he cannot see through a phone screen.
She may be raising children alone.
Managing bills.
Making difficult decisions.
Fighting exhaustion.
Attending church without him.
Watching other couples sit together while she silently counts the months until he returns.
She may smile during video calls because she does not want him to worry.
Then cry after the call ends.
And perhaps nobody has asked how she is really doing.
Everybody praises her sacrifice.
Everybody admires her strength.
Everybody tells her to be patient.
But very few people acknowledge how lonely faithfulness can feel.
And in that loneliness, sexual desire can become tangled with grief, longing, anxiety, and the ache of missing someone she deeply loves.
This does not mean every sexual response is morally justified.
It means we should understand the human being before issuing a verdict.
Jesus consistently demonstrated that kind of moral seriousness joined with compassion.
Consider the woman brought before Him in John 8.
She was publicly accused of adultery.
The crowd wanted condemnation.
Jesus did not declare adultery acceptable.
But neither did He join the crowd's eagerness to destroy her.
After her accusers departed, He said:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more." (John 8:11, ESV)
Grace did not erase holiness.
Holiness did not erase mercy.
Jesus refused both cheap permission and merciless condemnation.
That matters because some women reading this are not merely asking a theological question.
They are carrying years of shame.
Perhaps you were taught that every sexual feeling outside the physical presence of your husband was dirty.
Perhaps you were told that a truly godly woman would never struggle with sexual temptation.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that holiness means never having a body that asks for anything.
And now, because you are lonely and human, you are afraid to pray.
You wonder whether God is disgusted with you.
You promise never to struggle again.
Then the loneliness returns.
And so does the shame.
If that describes you, please hear this carefully.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction identifies sin and calls us toward repentance and restored fellowship with God.
Condemnation, in the crushing sense addressed by Romans 8:1, tells those who belong to Christ that they remain under the final guilty verdict from which Jesus has delivered them.
Paul writes:
The Greek word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation or an adverse judicial sentence.
Paul is not claiming that Christians never sin or never need correction.
He is declaring the extraordinary reality of justification and freedom from condemnation in Christ.
If you have sinned, the answer is not to pretend it was harmless.
The answer is to confess it, turn toward God, and trust the mercy made available through Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (ESV)
And if you are struggling with a question Scripture does not explicitly settle, you do not need to manufacture guilt simply to prove that you take holiness seriously.
You need wisdom.
You need an informed conscience.
You need prayer.
You need honest engagement with Scripture.
And you may need a compassionate conversation with your husband or a trusted, mature Christian counselor.
Romans 14 offers important principles concerning conscience and disputed practices, although Paul is addressing matters such as food and religious observances rather than masturbation.
Its principles should therefore be applied thoughtfully, not treated as a direct ruling on sexual ethics.
Romans 14:23 warns against acting in violation of one's faith-informed conviction.
That should encourage humility.
If you sincerely believe a behavior dishonors God, do not force yourself to do it merely because someone online says it is permissible.
But if another Christian reaches a different conclusion on a question Scripture does not directly address, be careful about claiming absolute biblical certainty where the text does not provide it.
Your conscience matters.
And your conscience must continually be shaped by truth rather than fear alone.
There is another passage we should not overlook.
First Corinthians 6:12 says:
"All things are lawful for me," but not all things are helpful. "All things are lawful for me," but I will not be dominated by anything. (ESV)
Paul is responding to a claim about freedom, not granting unrestricted permission for every behavior.
His point includes the importance of refusing to be mastered by one's appetites.
This offers a useful question for sexual self-examination.
Is this becoming something that controls me?
Not every repeated behavior is an addiction.
Not every sexual desire is a spiritual emergency.
But when a habit begins to interfere with sleep, responsibilities, relationships, peace of mind, or the ability to exercise self-control, it deserves attention.
If masturbation becomes tied to pornography, secrecy, compulsive escape, or a persistent withdrawal from marital intimacy, those patterns should be addressed honestly.
Not because your body is evil.
But because your body and your marriage deserve wise stewardship.
And perhaps the deeper issue is not what happens during one lonely evening.
Perhaps it is what happens during the hundreds of ordinary moments when husband and wife stop communicating about what separation is doing to them.
A husband can send money faithfully while forgetting to send tenderness.
A wife can remain sexually exclusive while silently building resentment.
Both can appear committed while slowly becoming strangers.
And neither may notice the distance growing until the day they are finally reunited and discover that physical proximity does not automatically restore emotional intimacy.
This is why your marriage needs more than rules about what not to do.
It needs intentional love.
It needs honest conversations about loneliness.
It needs reassurance without ridicule.
It needs shared prayer.
It needs practical plans for maintaining connection and, when possible, reunion.
It needs both spouses to recognize that prolonged separation can create genuine emotional and relational strain.
And it needs room for uncomfortable conversations without turning every confession into an accusation.
A wife should be able to say, "I'm struggling," without automatically being treated as unfaithful.
A husband should be able to express his convictions without automatically being accused of being controlling.
Both should be willing to listen.
Both should be willing to examine their assumptions.
Both should be willing to ask what genuine love requires.
Because the goal is not simply to survive until the next reunion.
The goal is to protect the covenant while you wait.
And if you are the husband reading this, there is something you need to hear too.
Your wife may be stronger than you realize.
But strength does not cancel loneliness.
She may understand why you have to work far away.
She may appreciate every sacrifice you make.
She may be proud of the way you provide for your family.
And still desperately miss being held.
Do not mistake her silence for the absence of need.
Do not assume that because she never complains, she never struggles.
Ask her how she is doing.
Then give her enough emotional safety to tell you the truth.
Not every problem can be solved by a phone call.
But being genuinely heard can make a painful season less isolating.
And wives, your husband's separation may carry its own burdens too.
He may be working long hours in an unfamiliar place.
Missing milestones.
Eating alone.
Struggling with temptation.
Wondering whether the sacrifice is worth the years he cannot recover.
He needs compassion as well.
The purpose of this conversation is not to decide which spouse suffers more.
It is to remember that you are on the same side.
You are not enemies negotiating permission to be human.
You are husband and wife learning how to honor God under difficult circumstances.
And that brings us to a question even more important than whether masturbation can ever occur without violating a marriage covenant.
What does faithfulness look like when nobody is watching?
It looks like truthfulness.
It looks like guarding your heart.
It looks like refusing to nurture desires that pull you toward betrayal.
It looks like respecting your spouse's dignity.
It looks like being willing to discuss boundaries rather than hiding behind assumptions.
It looks like exercising self-control without turning self-control into self-hatred.
It looks like remembering that your marriage is not only about satisfying desires but about learning to love another person sacrificially.
And above all, it looks like bringing your entire life before Jesus Christ.
Not merely your church attendance.
Not merely your public reputation.
Not merely the parts of your story that sound respectable.
Your loneliness too.
Your questions.
Your desires.
Your mistakes.
Your fears.
The things you are afraid to say aloud.
The places where you need wisdom.
The places where you need repentance.
The places where you need healing.
Jesus is not surprised that embodied human beings struggle.
Hebrews 4:15 describes Him as our High Priest who has been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
That does not mean Jesus experienced every identical circumstance or every particular sexual struggle.
It means He is not distant from human weakness and temptation.
The next verse invites believers to approach God's throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and help.
Think about that.
Not the throne of humiliation.
Not the throne of public embarrassment.
The throne of grace.
The Greek phrase θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος (thronō tēs charitos) means "throne of grace."
And the invitation is to come for mercy and timely help.
So if you are wrestling with sexual desire during a long separation, bring the question into God's presence.
You do not have to pretend that your body has stopped feeling.
You do not have to invent a biblical prohibition to prove your devotion.
You do not have to dismiss your conscience to escape discomfort.
And you do not have to treat your marriage vows as irrelevant simply because your husband is far away.
You can pursue truth and holiness without surrendering to shame.
You can recognize desire without being ruled by it.
You can acknowledge loneliness without allowing it to become an excuse for betrayal.
You can seek marital intimacy without reducing marriage to physical satisfaction.
And where you have genuinely sinned, you can repent without believing that your story is finished.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people never struggle.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is the center of everything.
Not sexual perfection.
Not an impressive religious reputation.
Not the ability to pretend you never feel temptation.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling people to repentance, faith, forgiveness, and new life.
And this is where our theme becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because Jesus calls evil good.
Not because grace makes obedience unnecessary.
Not because repentance can be replaced with comforting words.
But because Jesus meets people in the truth of their condition and offers what they cannot manufacture for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Restoration.
A new beginning.
A transformed heart.
A life no longer defined by its worst moments.
Maybe the scandal in your story is not adultery.
Maybe it is the private shame you have carried for years.
Maybe it is the fear that God will reject you for having questions you were never allowed to ask.
Maybe it is the silent distance growing between you and the person you promised to love.
Maybe it is the discovery that you have been trying to manage loneliness without ever telling anyone how much you are hurting.
Whatever it is, bring it into the light.
Not every private struggle needs to become a public confession.
You are entitled to dignity and appropriate privacy.
But secrecy that protects harmful patterns is different from privacy that respects healthy boundaries.
You can seek help without exposing intimate details to the entire world.
You can speak honestly with your spouse.
You can ask a trusted pastor or qualified Christian counselor for guidance.
You can pray for wisdom without assuming that every difficult feeling is evidence of spiritual failure.
And you can take your marriage seriously enough to have the conversations you have been avoiding.
Perhaps tonight, instead of asking only, "Am I allowed to do this?" you might ask:
"Lord, what is happening in my heart?"
"Am I seeking comfort in a way that honors You?"
"Am I allowing anything to control me?"
"Am I protecting trust between my husband and me?"
"Do I need to repent of something?"
"Do I need to stop condemning myself for something Your Word has not clearly condemned?"
"Do I need to tell my husband how lonely I have become?"
Those questions may not produce a convenient one-sentence answer.
But they can lead to something better.
Spiritual maturity.
And maturity does not always mean having fewer questions.
Sometimes it means finally learning to ask the right ones.
So let us answer the original question as clearly as Scripture allows.
Does masturbation while your husband is away automatically constitute adultery or betrayal of your marriage?
The Bible does not explicitly classify every act of masturbation as adultery.
It does, however, clearly call Christians to sexual holiness, faithfulness, self-control, purity of heart, and love within marriage.
Whether a particular act involves lustful fantasy, pornography, dishonesty, compulsive behavior, or violation of marital commitments can affect its moral significance.
Christian traditions also differ on whether masturbation itself is permissible, even without those additional concerns.
For that reason, it would be irresponsible to announce either that every instance is necessarily marital betrayal or that every instance is unquestionably acceptable to God.
The faithful response is not careless permission.
It is not automatic condemnation.
It is serious biblical discernment, prayerful conscience, honest marital communication, and a willingness to obey Christ even when obedience is difficult.
And please remember this.
You are not less of a Christian woman because you miss your husband's touch.
You are not less devoted because prolonged separation is painful.
You are not spiritually inferior because you need affection, reassurance, or closeness.
But neither should you allow legitimate desires to become the unquestioned authority over your decisions.
Jesus remains Lord over the whole of life.
Including the parts we rarely discuss in church.
Especially those parts.
If this article has brought a question into the light that you have carried in silence, I want to invite you into a conversation that is honest without being humiliating.
You do not need to reveal private sexual experiences in a public comment.
But perhaps you can share what this discussion has taught you about grace, faithfulness, or the importance of talking honestly with your spouse.
And if you have walked through years of separation and found ways to protect your marriage, your testimony may encourage another couple who is struggling tonight.
What helped you remain emotionally connected?
What conversations do you wish you had started sooner?
How has your faith sustained you through loneliness?
Your answer may remind someone that they are not alone.

If you know a wife whose husband is working overseas, a military spouse waiting for a reunion, or a couple trying to keep their marriage strong across thousands of miles, consider sharing this article privately with them.
Not to expose anyone.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because silence sometimes leaves struggling believers with only shame, confusion, and misinformation.
A difficult conversation may become the beginning of a healthier season.
Because the church does not need more people pretending they never struggle.
It needs people who are learning to bring their struggles honestly before Christ.
Not because a payment makes someone more faithful than another believer.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and lives increasingly transformed by His grace.
One way you may freely choose to express that generosity is by helping sustain and expand Gospel Warrior.
Biblically, giving should be willing, not coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." (ESV)
It is an additional, voluntary way to help a ministry continue reaching people.
If you are able and willing to help sustain this work, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
You do not have to pay to belong among people who are seeking Christ.
You do not have to purchase anything to receive the grace of God.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Our calling is to proclaim it faithfully.
And perhaps that is the most important reminder to carry away from this entire conversation.

Whether you are the lonely wife staring at an empty pillow, the husband working far from home, or the believer quietly wrestling with questions nobody taught you how to answer, your deepest hope is not found in winning an argument about a difficult sexual question.
Your deepest hope is Jesus.
The One who calls us to holiness without denying our humanity.
The One who exposes sin without taking pleasure in our humiliation.
The One who offers forgiveness without pretending sin does not matter.
The One who restores what shame tells us can never be restored.
So protect your marriage.
Guard your heart.
Speak the truth.
Seek wisdom.
Repent wherever repentance is needed.
Receive grace where grace is offered.
And remember that the distance between you and your husband does not have to become a distance between you and God.
Tonight, that empty side of the bed may still be empty.
The longing may still be real.
The reunion may still be months away.
But you can bring your questions, your loneliness, your conscience, and your entire heart before the Savior who knows you completely.
And the most beautiful thing about being fully known by Jesus is that you no longer have to hide in order to come home to His grace.
